body:
When you just look at section 3, it is non-obvious that "must" here is talking about document conformance and not implementation requirements. The conformance requirement is real and exists for a reason: some of the functionality that the id attribute enables, like fragment linking, only work properly when it's unique. On the other hand, implementations have to be able to interoperate on non-conforming documents, which is why the spec tells browsers how to behave even in non-unique cases. 

Section 1.11 goes into the difference between conformance requirements and implementation. 1.11.3 even has a line about this specific case.

I think the casual use of "must" to describe either a conformance or implementation requirement can be a real source of confusion, but I don't know what could be done about it without making the spec needlessly verbose.

Why can't the spec just say effectively "ids do not have to be unique but `<label for="(id)">` and `<a href="#(id)">` etc... will go to the first matching id on the page. Vs saying non-unique ids are "not conforming" even though the several of the most popular sites on the internet are using that exact feature?

@pshaughn's explanation is exactly correct. As such we can close this issue.

Regarding making it clearer when requirements apply to authors vs. implementers, I thought we had an open issue on that but I can't find it... it's indeed a hard problem.

> Why can't the spec just say effectively...

The goal of the spec is to guide you in avoiding the problems that come with such an approach. You can learn more about that in the sections @pshaughn referenced in their comment.

I read the section referenced by @pshaughn, here it is repeated. Which part are you refering to? --- # [](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#restrictions-on-content-models-and-on-attribute-values)1.11.3 Restrictions on content models and on attribute values *This [section](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-section-element) is non-normative.* Beyond the syntax of the language, this specification also places restrictions on how elements and attributes can be specified. These restrictions are present for similar reasons: ## Errors involving content with dubious semantics To avoid misuse of elements with defined meanings, content models are defined that restrict how elements can be nested when such nestings would be of dubious value. > For example, this specification disallows nesting a section element inside a [kbd](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-kbd-element) element, since it is highly unlikely for an author to indicate that an entire section sho[ul](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-ul-element)d be keyed in. ## Errors that involve a conf[li](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-li-element)ct in expressed semantics Similarly, to draw the author's attention to mistakes in the use of elements, clear contradictions in the semantics expressed are also considered conformance errors. > In the fragments below, for example, the semantics are nonsensical: a separator cannot sim[ul](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-ul-element)taneously be a cell, nor can a radio button be a progress bar. > > ``` >
> > ``` > > Another example is the restrictions on the content models of the ul element, which only allows [li](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-li-element) element children. Lists by definition consist just of zero or more list items, so if a ul element contains something other than an li element, it's not clear what was meant. ## Cases where the default styles are likely to lead to confusion Certain elements have default styles or behaviors that make certain combinations likely to lead to confusion. Where these have equivalent alternatives without this problem, the confusing combinations are disallowed. > For example, [div](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-div-element) elements are rendered as [block boxes](https://drafts.csswg.org/css2/#block-boxes%E2%91%A0), and [span](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-span-element) elements as [inline boxes](https://drafts.csswg.org/css2/#inline-box). Putting a [block box](https://drafts.csswg.org/css2/#block-boxes%E2%91%A0) in an [inline box](https://drafts.csswg.org/css2/#inline-box) is unnecessarily confusing; since either nesting just [div](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-div-element) elements, or nesting just [span](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-span-element) elements, or nesting [span](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-span-element) elements inside [div](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-div-element) elements all serve the same purpose as nesting a [div](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-div-element) element in a [span](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-span-element) element, but only the latter involves a [block box](https://drafts.csswg.org/css2/#block-boxes%E2%91%A0) in an [inline box](https://drafts.csswg.org/css2/#inline-box), the latter combination is disallowed. > Another example would be the way [interactive content](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#interactive-content-2) cannot be nested. For example, a [button](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-button-element) element cannot contain a [textarea](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-textarea-element) element. This is because the default behavior of such nesting interactive elements would be highly confusing to users. Instead of nesting these elements, they can be placed side by side. ## Errors that indicate a likely misunderstanding of the specification Sometimes, something is disallowed because allowing it would likely cause author confusion. > For example, setting the [disabled](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#attr-fe-disabled) attribute to the value "false" is disallowed, because despite the appearance of meaning that the element is enabled, it in fact means that the element is disabled (what matters for implementations is the presence of the attribute, not its value). # Errors involving limits that have been imposed merely to simplify the language Some conformance errors simplify the language that authors need to learn. > For example, the [area](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-area-element) element's [shape](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#attr-area-shape) attribute, despite accepting both [circ](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#attr-area-shape-keyword-circ) and [circle](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#attr-area-shape-keyword-circle) values in practice as synonyms, disallows the use of the [circ](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#attr-area-shape-keyword-circ) value, so as to simplify tutorials and other learning aids. There would be no benefit to allowing both, but it would cause extra confusion when teaching the language. # Errors that involve peculiarities of the parser Certain elements are parsed in somewhat eccentric ways (typically for historical reasons), and their content model restrictions are intended to avoid exposing the author to these issues. > For example, a [form](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-form-element) element isn't allowed inside [phrasing content](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#phrasing-content-2), because when parsed as HTML, a [form](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-form-element) element's start tag will im[p](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-p-element)ly a p element's end tag. Thus, the following markup results in two [paragraphs](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#paragraph), not one: > > ``` >

Welcome.

> ``` > > It is parsed exactly like the following: > > ``` >

Welcome.

> ``` ## Errors that would likely result in scripts failing in hard-to-debug ways Some errors are intended to help prevent script problems that would be hard to debug. > This is why, for instance, it is non-conforming to have two [id](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-id-attribute) attributes with the same value. Duplicate IDs lead to the wrong element being selected, with sometimes disastrous effects whose cause is hard to determine. ## Errors that waste authoring time Some constructs are disallowed because historically they have been the cause of a lot of wasted authoring time, and by encouraging authors to avoid making them, authors can save time in future efforts. > For example, a [script](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-script-element) element's [src](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#attr-script-src) attribute causes the element's contents to be ignored. However, this isn't obvious, especially if the element's contents appear to be executable [script](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-script-element) — which can lead to authors spending a lot of time trying to debug the inline script without realizing that it is not executing. To reduce this problem, this specification makes it non-conforming to have executable script in a script element when the [src](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#attr-script-src) attribute is present. This means that authors who are validating their documents are less likely to waste time with this kind of mistake. ## Errors that involve areas that affect authors migrating between the HTML and XML syntaxes Some authors like to write files that can be interpreted as both XML and HTML with similar results. Though this practice is discouraged in general due to the myriad of subtle complications involved (especially when involving scripting, styling, or any kind of automated serialization), this specification has a few restrictions intended to at least somewhat mitigate the difficulties. This makes it easier for authors to use this as a transitionary step when migrating between the HTML and XML syntaxes. > For example, there are somewhat complicated rules surrounding the [lang](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#attr-lang) and [xml:lang](https://www.w3.org/TR/xml/#sec-lang-tag) attributes intended to keep the two synchronized. > Another example would be the restrictions on the values of xmlns attributes in the HTML serialization, which are intended to ensure that elements in conforming documents end up in the same namespaces whether processed as HTML or XML. ## Errors that involve areas reserved for future expansion As with the restrictions on the syntax intended to allow for new syntax in future revisions of the language, some restrictions on the content models of elements and values of attributes are intended to allow for future expansion of the HTML vocabulary. > For example, limiting the values of the [target](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#attr-hyperlink-target) attribute that start with an U+005F LOW LINE character (_) to only specific predefined values allows new predefined values to be introduced at a future time without conflicting with author-defined values. ## Errors that indicate a mis-use of other specifications Certain restrictions are intended to support the restrictions made by other specifications. > For example, requiring that attributes that take media query lists use only valid media query lists reinforces the importance of following the conformance rules of that specification.

Probably a mix of "Errors that indicate a likely misunderstanding of the specification", "Errors that would likely result in scripts failing in hard-to-debug ways", and "Errors that waste authoring time
